title: A pricing page for a developer-tool company
excerpt: Engineers open pricing to judge fit. Show the unit, what is included, what is not, and how to try the product. Do not hide a number they will ask for.
alt: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window. The article is about a pricing page someone can check while they are already in the work.
caption: The price should be readable in the same sitting as the work. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a developer-tool pricing page show?
faqs.answer: Show the unit, such as seats, usage, or a hosted project, and a plan you recommend for a typical start. List what is included and what is absent in the same view. Say how to try the product, including what the trial will not ask for.

faqs.question: How should free and paid plans differ in public?
faqs.answer: State the difference beside the price. Name the limit that bites, such as events, retention, or where the tool runs. Leave roadmap features off the table until they ship in the build people can try.

faqs.question: Is contact sales acceptable on a pricing page?
faqs.answer: Use it for a plan that is actually a contract, and still show the shape of that price. Do not put it on the free column. A blank enterprise cell gives a skeptical reader a reason to leave rather than a reason to book.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A developer-tool company pricing page is where an engineer who is skeptical of marketing judges fit. They can multiply. They opened the page to see what is included, what is not, and how to try the product before anyone sends an invoice. Show that shape. If they will ask the price on a call anyway, hiding it only spends the call on a number you could have printed.

A table that performs generosity and omits the unit is a slogan in grid form. Name the unit. Seats, usage, pipelines, or a hosted project. Then show the door to a trial that matches the page. The try path and the price are one conversation.

## The shape, before the total

Put the unit in the first screen. Per seat, per month, with a free tier that includes a named limit. Or usage, metered on events, with a published rate and a ceiling that triggers a conversation. Or a paid cloud and a free self-hosted build, if both exist. The engineer is sorting themselves into a shape. Help them sort.

Recommend a starting plan in a sentence. "A single team running it in CI starts here." The recommendation is guidance, not a dark pattern. They can still read the other columns. They should not have to reverse-engineer which column is real.

If the open-source build and the paid build differ, say the difference beside the price, not in a blog post from last year. What the free build runs. What the paid build adds. Where the telemetry lives. This buyer will look. Write the answer where they are looking.

Nielsen Norman Group notes that people often read only about a quarter of the text on pages they open. A pricing page that spends the top on a manifesto will have its unit skipped. Lead with the unit. The philosophy can be one sentence under it, if the sentence changes the fit. "No charge for public projects" changes the fit. "We believe in fair pricing" does not.

## What the plan includes

List what they receive in the words they use. Private repositories. Retention of traces. SSO. Audit log. Support that is a human, a forum, or a document. Seats that include viewers, or seats that do not. Say which.

Make the rows comparable. If the team plan includes SSO and the free plan does not, show the absence. Hiding the row on the cheaper plan reads as a trick once they toggle. A plain "not included" respects the reader who is trying to say no as much as the reader who is trying to say yes.

Include the limits that bite. Events per month. Users who can edit. Projects before a hard stop. Retention days. Engineers buy limits. They have been burned by unlimited that meant unusable. A number is kinder than an adjective.

Say where it runs. Your cloud, their VPC, their laptop. A price that omits the runtime is an incomplete price. The bill and the architecture arrive together in their mind. Let them arrive together on the page.

## What the plan does not include

Write the exclusions in the same view as the price. Implementation of their pipeline. A custom parser for a private format. On-call for their incidents. Training for a department. If those are separate paid work, point to that offer with a boundary. If they are not offered, say they are not offered.

Support level is an exclusion even when you would rather talk about community. "Forum on the free plan. Email on the paid plan. A named engineer is a separate agreement." That sentence prevents a trial user from arriving angry, and it prevents a sales call from redefining the page.

Data is an exclusion worth a line. What you store. How long. Whether a self-hosted install sends anything home. An engineer who is skeptical of marketing is often skeptical of quiet telemetry. The pricing page is a fair place to be dull and exact. Exact is the tone they trust.

If a feature is on the roadmap and not in the build, leave it off the pricing table. Roadmap rows are how pricing pages become fiction. Ship, then add the row. The page should match the version they can try today.

## Try the product from the price

Each plan that can be tried should say how. A button to the sandbox. A command. A free org with the stated limit. The label should match the homepage, so the site has one verb for the trial. Changing "install" to "start for free" to "talk to us" across three plans is fine only when the mechanisms truly differ. When they differ, say the mechanism.

Do not put "contact sales" on every column including the free one. The free column should start. The column that is genuinely a contract can ask for a conversation, and it should still show the unit. "From a named minimum" or "priced on events above a threshold" gives them a reason to book. A blank enterprise cell gives them a reason to leave.

Tell them what the trial will not ask. No card for the sandbox. Or a card that is not charged until the limit, if that is true. Say the true version. This reader will test the sentence against the signup flow within the hour. If the flow contradicts the page, the page is what they will remember.

A demo can sit as a secondary path for a security review or a procurement packet. Label it as that. Do not let it become the only way to learn a number that is already public. Engineers share pricing pages in chat. A page that requires a meeting to be understood does not travel.

## Usage, seats, and the plan that lies by mixing them

Pick a primary unit and stick to it in the first screen. A price that is seats plus usage plus a platform fee can be honest and still unreadable if you introduce all three as equals. Show the unit they will hit first. Explain the others in the next short block, with an example that uses round numbers.

Give one worked example. "A team of eight, one private project, under the event cap, pays this." Keep the example boring and labeled as an example. A calculator with twelve inputs can live behind a disclosure for the person modeling a year. It should not be the first thing a skeptical reader has to operate.

Watch the annual toggle. If monthly is real, show it. If annual is the only contract you sign, say that monthly is unavailable or is a trial length. A toggle that resets the story is a dark pattern this audience will screenshot.

Watch the word unlimited. If a fair-use policy exists, the policy is the price. Link it in the same cell. Unlimited with a surprise enforcement email is how trust dies after the purchase, and this buyer has group chats for that story.

## Publish only what you can invoice

Read the page next to the billing code or the order form. Platform fees, overages, and the definition of a seat should match. If finance and the website disagree, the website is the thing a stranger sees first. Fix it before they forward it.

Date the page in a quiet line if prices change often. "These figures match the public price as of the current docs." You do not need a legal essay. You need a reader to know the table is maintained. A stale table is a form of hiding.

Google's guidance on people-first content fits this page tightly. Answer the question they brought, from facts you have, without filler. The question is "what would we pay, and what would we get, and can I try it first?" Three answers. Then stop.

Check the title. It should say pricing, plainly, so a shared link is obvious in a thread. Clever titles waste the one moment a busy engineer decides to open the tab.

Check the numbers against the sandbox. If the free tier on the page and the limit inside the product differ by even one rule, fix the page or fix the product before you announce either. This reader will create the project and look. A mismatch becomes the story they tell, and the story is more memorable than the type scale you debated. Agreement is the design.

## A page a skeptical reader can skim

Use this order and resist a brand film at the top.

1. The unit and who it is for.
2. The plan you recommend, with included and excluded in view.
3. The limit that matters.
4. How to try the product, including what the try will not ask.
5. One example in round numbers.
6. The contract path, only for the plan that is actually a contract, with the shape still visible.

Read it aloud to someone who would use the tool. Ask them which plan they would start on, and what would make them write to you. If they cannot answer, the shape is still hidden. Add a fact. Do not add an adjective.

When the price is legible, the next confusion is often a services offer written as "partnership." Engineers want a boundary. Read [how to describe services so the next step is still to try the product](/blog/the-services-page-a-developer-tool-company-actually-needs) before you add a row of abstract help under the table.

If you want a second look at a page that has to be exact, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the table and the signup flow. The work is making them agree.
